content:
Look, I mean no disrespect to the Apple Vision Pro. The Apple Vision Pro is definitely a great product. But the iPhone Duo and the Apple Vision Pro are not even in the same conversation.

There's a school of thought that the iPhone Duo might face the same issues as the Apple Vision Pro. The reasoning is that based on its pricing and device-specific software, it might be a critical darling but a commercial flop. But the two simply cannot be compared.

The iPhone Duo doesn't have to deal with the Apple Vision Pro's biggest pitfall

The biggest problem with this view is that the Apple Vision Pro doesn't replace a core device. It can act as a portable cinema, a better gaming display, and the mixed reality experience is genuinely moving.

The Apple Vision Pro does not replace your iPhone or iPad. It's an immersive world you can put in your carry-on, but it's fundamentally a stationary device, not a small tablet you can slip in your pocket and pull out anywhere.

Then there's the pricing. The iPhone Duo's starting price of $1,999 is not cheap, but it's less outrageous than you might think. Consumers are willing to pay for a premium smartphone because phones are simply too important in modern life.

The Apple Vision Pro's original starting price of $3,499 was never exactly approachable, and it's now been hiked to $3,669. That's almost enough to buy two iPhone Duos, pushing it into iPhone Quattro territory.

Utility, portability, and affordability combined form the biggest differentiator. The Apple Vision Pro hasn't managed to become a mainstream consumer product in any of these areas, which makes it hard for the device to truly live up to its full potential.

The iPhone Duo combines iPhone and small iPad into one device

The iPhone Duo combines the utility of an iPhone and a small iPad, and it still fits in your pocket. The pricing works out like buying an iPhone 16 Pro this year and then upgrading to the iPhone 17 Pro next year — it's a spending pattern people can actually get behind.

Yes, the iPhone Duo will definitely face an uphill battle with software optimization, at least when it comes to third-party apps. But Apple has already built a fairly comprehensive narrative around its OS and first-party apps. Developers will quickly get the tools they need to build great apps for that versatile folding display.

For me, the iPhone Duo's biggest challenge is that it's still not a true no-compromise iPhone yet. Hopefully future versions can achieve that.

The hardware is still solid and the OS experience is smooth too. But until it can run iPad apps (which isn't as complicated as some make it out to be), it can't claim to unfold into an iPad. And the thing costs £2,000 with the same camera specs as the 16e — that's a tough sell. Compared to its foldable rivals, the value just doesn't hold up when you factor in practicality. It's not Apple's best in any of the categories it occupies.

These aren't 'first-gen growing pains.' Apple should be ahead of Samsung, Honor, and Google across the board, but it chose not to be.

Combining all of the iPhone's best specs with a folding display would obviously be a beautiful thing. But as it stands, the iPhone 18 Pro still reigns supreme when it comes to photography and Face ID.

Importantly, for a group of consumers who want to try out this new iPhone form factor, none of those trade-offs will be a barrier.

Ultimately, the Apple Vision Pro should be seriously envious of the iPhone Duo's 'problems.'
